newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean troops up manhunt for N.Korean agents.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean troops up manhunt for N.Korean agents.

text.p: Thousands of South Korean troops on Thursday combed rugged woodlands on the east coast in search of North Korean agents suspected of strangling an elderly woman and shooting dead two other South Koreans.

Soldiers stopped cars at check points around Mt Odea where the three bodies were found on Wednesday. The mountain is about 70 km (44 miles) northwest of the point where 26 North Korean troops came ashore from a grounded submarine last month.

Twenty-two of the North Korean infiltrators have been killed by South Korean soldiers or found dead. One was captured alive. The search for the remaining three had slowly begun to wind down until Wednesday.
Seoul suspects the missing North Korean agents are responsible for the deaths of the three civilians. The alarm was raised after the trio failed to return from picking wild mushrooms on Tuesday.

The bodies were covered with grass and surrounded by empty M-16 rifle cartridges with no serial markings. The 67-year-old woman had been strangled and bludgeoned with a heavy implement while the two men, aged 54 and 45, had been shot.
Some of the North Koreans who came ashore from the submarine, found stranded on rocks on September 18, were carrying M-16 rifles.
The murders have deepened a current crisis on the Korean peninsula over the submarine incident.

Pyongyang said the submarine drifted into South Korean waters after encountering engine trouble and has threatened "merciless retaliation" for the deaths of its soldiers. It is demanding the return of the bodies of the dead North Koreans and the survivors along with the vessel.
Winston Lord, U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for East Asia and Pacific Affairs, was due to arrive in Seoul later on Thursday on a three-day visit to discuss the crisis.
A fragile ceasefire has kept the peace on the Korean peninsula since the 1950-53 Korean War.
